title: Character Analysis
content_html:
Characters as Vehicles for Theme

In The Empress, Gupta creates characters who are both individual human beings and representatives of broader historical experiences. For the Edexcel exam, you need to analyse characters on both levels: what they are like as people (AO1) and what they represent about the Empire, race, and power (AO3/AO4). This lesson examines the play’s five most important characters and how Gupta uses each to develop her themes.

Rani — Hope, Vulnerability, and Resilience

Rani is the emotional heart of the play. She arrives in London full of optimism and curiosity, making her a sympathetic figure from the start. Gupta uses Rani’s journey to dramatise the cycle of hope, betrayal, and resilience that defined the experience of many Indian women in Victorian Britain.

What makes Rani a compelling character is that she does not remain a passive victim. After her abandonment, she develops awareness of the system that has exploited her and finds strength in solidarity with the other ayahs. Her character arc moves from individual hope to collective resistance. Gupta presents Rani as resourceful and intelligent — the system fails her, not the other way round.

Key Fact

Rani’s character arc — from hope through betrayal to resilience — is the play’s emotional spine. Gupta uses her journey to show that the Empire’s victims were not passive: they suffered, they endured, and they found ways to resist. Rani’s resilience is political as well as personal.

Abdul — Loyalty and Quiet Strength

Abdul, Rani’s husband, represents a quieter form of resistance. Where Hari is vocal and politically active, Abdul demonstrates quiet strength — enduring hardship while protecting those around him. Gupta uses Abdul to show that resistance takes many forms, and that the everyday act of surviving in a hostile system is itself an act of courage.

Abdul also functions as a foil to Hari. Where Hari becomes increasingly angry and politicised, Abdul maintains a more pragmatic approach, focused on immediate survival. Gupta does not present either response as superior — both are understandable reactions to injustice.

The contrast between Abdul and Hari represents a real debate within colonised communities: is it better to work within the system or to challenge it directly? Abdul’s pragmatism keeps him and Rani alive, but it does not change the system. Hari’s anger drives political awareness, but it also puts him at risk. Gupta presents both approaches with sympathy, allowing the audience to evaluate them through AO4. This dual response mirrors historical reality — Indian communities in Victorian Britain contained both moderates and radicals.

Hari — Anger and Political Voice

Hari is the play’s most politically vocal character. As a lascar facing brutal working conditions, he develops from a frustrated worker into an articulate critic of the Empire. Gupta uses Hari to give voice to the argument that Indian people deserve not charity but equal rights and justice.

Hari’s character serves an important structural function. He connects the personal stories of exploitation to the broader political argument. Without Hari, the play would be a story of individual suffering; with him, it becomes a critique of an entire system. His growing political consciousness mirrors the historical development of Indian political movements in Britain.

Key Fact

Hari transforms the play from personal stories into political theatre. His anger is not random — it grows directly from his experience of exploitation. Gupta uses him to show that political consciousness emerges from lived injustice, not abstract ideology.

Mrs Phelps — Embodying Victorian Racism

Mrs Phelps is the play’s most prominent British character and the one who most clearly embodies Victorian attitudes towards Indian people. She is not a villain in the traditional sense — she does not set out to be cruel. Instead, her racism is casual, habitual, and built into her worldview. She genuinely believes she is being kind to the ayahs, even as she treats them as less than human.

Gupta’s most sophisticated choice with Mrs Phelps is making her racism ordinary rather than extreme. Mrs Phelps is not a cartoon villain — she is a recognisable type. Her condescension, her assumption of superiority, and her ability to discard Indian people without guilt are all presented as normal within Victorian society. This makes her more disturbing than an overtly cruel character would be, because it shows that racism does not require malice — it only requires a system that normalises inequality.

For AO4, consider whether Mrs Phelps is personally responsible for her attitudes, or whether she is simply a product of her society. Gupta seems to suggest both: Mrs Phelps is shaped by the system, but she also has the choice to see the ayahs as human beings, and she consistently fails to make that choice.

Dadabhai Naoroji — Working Within the System

Naoroji represents the possibility of using Britain’s own political system to challenge its injustices. His election as Britain’s first Asian MP in 1892 is the play’s most concrete symbol of hope. Gupta presents him as dignified, intelligent, and determined — a counter to the racist stereotypes applied to Indian people by characters like Mrs Phelps.

However, Gupta does not present Naoroji as a simple hero. His success is limited — one MP cannot dismantle an empire — and the racist opposition he faces (including Lord Salisbury’s contempt) shows that political progress is slow and contested. Naoroji represents the hope that the system can be changed from within, but Gupta leaves open the question of whether this hope is justified.

Queen Victoria never appears on stage, yet she is the play’s most powerful character. Her title gives the play its name; her proclamation is referenced in Act 3; her empire creates the conditions that destroy the characters’ lives. Gupta’s decision to keep Victoria offstage is a deliberate structural choice. It mirrors how power operates: the most powerful people are often invisible, while the powerless bear the visible consequences of their decisions. Victoria’s absence is itself a form of dramatic commentary.
exam_tip_html: When writing about characters for Edexcel, always connect them to Gupta’s dramatic purpose. Don’t just describe what characters do — explain why Gupta created them this way. Use the formula: “Gupta uses [character] to [dramatic purpose], which [effect on audience].” For AO4, offer alternative readings: is Mrs Phelps personally cruel or just a product of her society? Is Hari’s anger constructive or self-destructive?
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rani’s character arc from hope through betrayal to resilience represents the broader experience of Indian women exploited by the Empire.
  • Hari and Abdul represent contrasting responses to injustice — political activism versus pragmatic survival — and Gupta presents both with sympathy.
  • Mrs Phelps embodies the banality of racism: her cruelty is casual and habitual, showing that the system did not require deliberate malice to destroy lives.

glossary_terms.definition: The play’s central female character, a young ayah whose journey from hope to disillusionment represents the broader experience of Indian women exploited by the British Empire.
The ability to maintain dignity and continue functioning despite suffering, without necessarily confronting the system directly.
A young Indian lascar in the play whose growing anger at exploitation transforms him into a political voice challenging the entire structure of the British Empire.
A British character in the play who represents Victorian paternalism — the belief that British people were doing Indians a favour by employing them, while treating them as fundamentally inferior.
A Parsi political figure from India who became the first Asian Member of Parliament in Britain, elected for Finsbury Central in 1892.
